title: Causal Inference by Simulation
text:
Preface
Six worked examples of causal-inference methods, each built on simulated data with a known true effect. That lets you check whether a method recovers the truth, and see how each assumption failure biases the answer.
The estimators live in a small, tested package, causalsimkit (see Appendix A — The causalsimkit package), rather than in the chapters, so they are reusable and the chapters stay readable. Each chapter ends with practical notes and pointers to production libraries.

title: Causal Inference by Simulation
text:
Choosing a method

Many treated units, clean comparison group with similar pre-trends → DiD (1  Difference-in-Differences (DiD)). Staggered timing → heterogeneity-robust event study (3  Event Studies, Part B).
One or a few treated aggregates (a market, a region) → synthetic control (2  Synthetic Control, and Choosing Between SC and DiD); choose vs DiD by backtest error.
Treatment set by a cutoff on a score → RDD (4  Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)).
Self-selected treatment, rich pre-treatment covariates → propensity / doubly robust methods (5  Propensity-Score Methods) + sensitivity analysis.
You control assignment but users interfere → randomize geos or time blocks (6  Geo Experiments and Switchback Testing).
Market reaction to news → financial event study (3  Event Studies, Part A).

title: 1  Difference-in-Differences (DiD)
text:
1.1 Pre-trend plot
Question: what did an intervention do to the treated group, relative to what would have happened without it?
DiD estimates the ATT1 by comparing the change in the treated group to the change in an untreated comparison group:
\[\widehat{ATT} = (\bar Y_{T,post} - \bar Y_{T,pre}) - (\bar Y_{C,post} - \bar Y_{C,pre}) \tag{1.1}\]
Plot the average outcome per group per period. Under parallel trends the lines are vertically offset but move together before the dashed line. In the right panel of Figure 1.1, the treated group is drifting away before treatment — any DiD estimate there will absorb that drift.
Code
def plot_group_means(df, ax, title):
    means = df.groupby(["period", "treated"])["y"].mean().unstack()
    ax.plot(means.index, means[1], "o-", label="treated")
    ax.plot(means.index, means[0], "s-", label="control")
    ax.axvline(TREAT_PERIOD - 0.5, ls="--", c="grey")
    ax.set(title=title, xlabel="period", ylabel="mean outcome")
    ax.legend()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4), sharey=True)
plot_group_means(good, axes[0], "Parallel trends hold")
plot_group_means(bad, axes[1], "Parallel trends violated (treated pre-trend)")
plt.show()








Figure 1.1: Raw group means when parallel trends hold (left) and when the treated group has a pre-trend (right). The dashed line marks the start of treatment.

title: 1  Difference-in-Differences (DiD)
text:
1.2 2×2 DiD and TWFE
The canonical regression is y ~ treated + post + treated:post. The interaction is the DiD estimate (Equation 1.1). TWFE replaces the group and period dummies with unit and period fixed effects — identical in a balanced block-adoption design, but it also absorbs unit-level heterogeneity and lets you add time-varying covariates.






ImportantCluster your standard errors



Always cluster standard errors at the unit level (the level at which treatment is assigned): outcomes within a unit are serially correlated, and ignoring that makes CIs far too narrow (Bertrand et al. 2004).



Bertrand, Marianne, Esther Duflo, and Sendhil Mullainathan. 2004. “How Much Should We Trust Differences-in-Differences Estimates?” Quarterly Journal of Economics.


Code
1r_2x2 = did.did_2x2(good, "y", "treated", "post", cluster="unit")
2r_twfe = did.twfe_did(good, "y", "unit", "period", "D")

pd.concat([
    r_2x2.summary(["treated:post"]).rename(index={"treated:post": "2x2 DiD"}),
    r_twfe.summary(["D"]).rename(index={"D": "TWFE"}),
]).assign(truth=TRUE_EFFECT)

title: 1  Difference-in-Differences (DiD)
text:
1.3 Event study: leads and lags
Instead of one post dummy, estimate one coefficient per period relative to treatment (period −1 is the omitted reference), as in Equation 1.2:
\[y_{it} = \alpha_i + \gamma_t + \sum_{k \neq -1} \beta_k \, \mathbb{1}[t - T_0 = k] \cdot \text{treated}_i + \varepsilon_{it} \tag{1.2}\]

Leads (\(k<0\)) should be ≈ 0. They are a direct visual + statistical check of pre-trends.
Lags (\(k \ge 0\)) trace out the dynamic effect: does it appear immediately, build up, or fade?

The joint F-test on the leads summarises the pre-trend check in one number.


Code
def add_rel_time(df):
    return df.assign(rel_time=np.where(df.treated == 1, df.period - TREAT_PERIOD, np.nan))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4), sharey=True)
for ax, (name, df) in zip(axes, {"Parallel trends hold": good, "Violated": bad}.items()):
    tab, res = did.event_study(add_rel_time(df), "y", "unit", "period", "rel_time", window=(-8, 7))
    wald = res.wald_test(did.lead_names(tab))
    ax.errorbar(tab.rel_time, tab.coef, yerr=1.96 * tab.se, fmt="o", capsize=3)
    ax.axhline(0, c="k", lw=0.8); ax.axhline(TRUE_EFFECT, c="green", ls=":", label="true effect")
    ax.axvline(-0.5, ls="--", c="grey")
    ax.set(title=f"{name}\npre-trend F-test p = {wald['p']:.3f}", xlabel="periods relative to treatment")
    ax.legend()
axes[0].set_ylabel("coefficient (95% CI)")
plt.show()








Figure 1.2: Event-study coefficients with 95% confidence intervals. Under parallel trends (left) the leads sit near zero and the lags near the true effect of 2.0; with a violated pre-trend (right) the leads slope upward.





In Figure 1.2, on the left the leads hover around zero and the lags sit on the true effect. On the right the leads slope upward and the F-test rejects — exactly the warning you want before trusting the post-period coefficients, which are now inflated by the continuing trend.


Code
r_bad = did.twfe_did(bad, "y", "unit", "period", "D")
print(f"TWFE estimate with violated parallel trends: {r_bad.params['D']:.2f} "
      f"(95% CI {r_bad.conf_int().loc['D', 'lower']:.2f} to {r_bad.conf_int().loc['D', 'upper']:.2f}); truth = {TRUE_EFFECT}")


TWFE estimate with violated parallel trends: 4.65 (95% CI 4.32 to 4.98); truth = 2.0

1.4 Placebo test: fake treatment date
Drop the real post-period, pretend treatment happened earlier, and re-estimate. A “significant effect” where none can exist means the design is picking up something other than the treatment.


Code
def placebo(df, fake_start):
    pre = df[df.period < TREAT_PERIOD].assign(D=lambda d: d.treated * (d.period >= fake_start))
    r = did.twfe_did(pre, "y", "unit", "period", "D")
    return {"fake_start": fake_start, "estimate": r.params["D"], "p": r.pvalues["D"]}

pd.DataFrame([placebo(good, s) | {"data": "parallel"} for s in (6, 8)]
             + [placebo(bad, s) | {"data": "violated"} for s in (6, 8)])

title: 1  Difference-in-Differences (DiD)
text:
1.5 Practical checklist



Table 1.3: Practical DiD checklist.









Check
Why




Raw pre-trend plot
Catches most problems before any regression.


Event-study leads ≈ 0 + joint F-test
Formalises the visual check.


Placebo dates / placebo outcomes
Guards against coincident shocks.


Cluster SEs at the treatment-assignment level
Serial correlation inflates false positives. With < ~30 clusters, use a wild cluster bootstrap.


No anticipation
If units react before \(T_0\) (announcements), move the reference period earlier.


Stable composition
Units entering/leaving the panel because of treatment breaks the comparison.












WarningCaveats worth knowing




Passing a pre-trend test is not proof. Pre-tests have low power, and conditioning on passing them distorts inference (Roth 2022). Report sensitivity bounds — e.g. HonestDiD (Rambachan and Roth 2023): “how large a post-period trend deviation would overturn the result?”
Staggered adoption (units treated at different times) breaks TWFE when effects vary over time or across cohorts. See Chapter 3.
Parallel trends is scale-dependent: if it holds in levels it generally won’t hold in logs. Choose the scale up front for substantive reasons.
When no comparison group tracks the treated unit, consider synthetic control (Chapter 2).




Rambachan, Ashesh, and Jonathan Roth. 2023. “A More Credible Approach to Parallel Trends.” Review of Economic Studies.






NoteProduction tools



pyfixest (fast high-dimensional FE, clustered/wild-bootstrap SEs, event studies), linearmodels.PanelOLS, statsmodels (smf.ols(...).fit(cov_type="cluster", ...)).

title: 1  Difference-in-Differences (DiD)
text:
1.6 Check your understanding






TipWhy can’t parallel trends be tested after treatment, and what do we check instead?





After treatment we never observe the treated group’s untreated outcomes, so the assumption is untestable there. We check the pre-period: the raw trend plot, event-study leads near zero with a joint F-test, and placebo dates. Passing is evidence, not proof, because pre-tests have low power (Roth 2022).




Roth, Jonathan. 2022. “Pretest with Caution: Event-Study Estimates After Testing for Parallel Trends.” American Economic Review: Insights.






TipWhy is the TWFE estimate above 2.0 when the pre-trend is violated?





The treated group was already drifting upward before treatment. DiD attributes the continuing drift to the treatment, so the post-period estimate is inflated.









ImportantTry it



In the first code cell change pretrend=0.25 to a smaller value such as 0.05 and re-render. At what drift does the lead F-test stop rejecting, and how biased is the TWFE estimate then?

title: 2  Synthetic Control, and Choosing Between SC and DiD
text:
2.1 Fit both counterfactuals
Setting: one (or a few) treated aggregate units — a city, a region, a market — and a donor pool of untreated units. Example: a pricing change launched only in one geographic market.
DiD would compare the treated market to the equal-weighted average of the donors. That only works if the average happens to share the treated market’s trend. Synthetic control instead learns weights so the weighted donor combination reproduces the treated market’s pre-period path (Equation 2.1):
\[\hat w = \arg\min_{w} \sum_{t < T_0} \Big(y_{1t} - \sum_j w_j y_{jt}\Big)^2 \quad \text{s.t. } w_j \ge 0,\ \sum_j w_j = 1 \tag{2.1}\]
The non-negativity and sum-to-one constraints keep the counterfactual an interpolation of real markets (no extrapolation) and typically make it sparse and interpretable.
Code
1sc = synth.synthetic_control(wide, TREATED, TREAT_TIME)
2dd = synth.did_counterfactual(wide, TREATED, TREAT_TIME)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4))
for res, c in ((sc, "C0"), (dd, "C1")):
    axes[0].plot(res.counterfactual, c=c, ls="--", label=f"{res.method} counterfactual")
    axes[1].plot(res.gap, c=c, label=res.method)
axes[0].plot(wide[TREATED], c="C3", lw=2, label="actual")
axes[1].axhline(TRUE_EFFECT, c="green", ls=":", label="true effect")
axes[1].axhline(0, c="k", lw=0.8)
for ax, t in zip(axes, ("Actual vs counterfactual", "Gap = actual − counterfactual")):
    ax.axvline(TREAT_TIME - 0.5, ls="--", c="grey"); ax.set(title=t, xlabel="period"); ax.legend()
plt.show()



1

Learns non-negative donor weights that sum to one and best reproduce the treated market’s pre-period path (Equation 2.1).

2

text:
2.2 Model selection: in-sample and out-of-sample fit
In-sample pre-period RMSPE always favours the more flexible method, so on its own it’s not a fair comparison. The backtest holds out the last h pre-treatment periods, fits on the rest, and scores the “forecast” on the held-out window where the true effect is zero. Pick the method with the lower out-of-sample error — the same logic as cross-validation, respecting time order.


Code
rows = []
for name, method in {"synthetic_control": synth.synthetic_control, "did": synth.did_counterfactual}.items():
    res = method(wide, TREATED, TREAT_TIME)
    row = {"method": name, "pre_rmspe (in-sample)": res.pre_rmspe}
    for h in (4, 6, 8):
        row[f"backtest_rmspe h={h}"] = synth.backtest(wide, TREATED, TREAT_TIME, h, method)
    row["ATT estimate"] = res.att
    rows.append(row)
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("method").assign(true_ATT=TRUE_EFFECT)

title: 2  Synthetic Control, and Choosing Between SC and DiD
text:
2.3 Inference: placebo-in-space
With one treated unit, conventional standard errors don’t apply. Instead, pretend each donor was treated, re-run SC, and ask: is the treated market’s post/pre RMSPE ratio extreme relative to the placebos? The permutation p-value is its rank. Using the ratio (not the raw post gap) penalises placebos that fit poorly pre-treatment.


Code
placebos = synth.placebo_in_space(wide, TREATED, TREAT_TIME, method=synth.synthetic_control)
p_val = synth.permutation_pvalue(placebos, TREATED)

# Common practice: hide placebos with very poor pre-fit when plotting (here > 5x the treated pre-RMSPE).
good_fit = placebos[placebos.pre_rmspe <= 5 * placebos.loc[TREATED, "pre_rmspe"]]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4))
for u, row in good_fit.iterrows():
    axes[0].plot(row.gap, c="C3" if u == TREATED else "lightgrey", lw=2.5 if u == TREATED else 0.8)
axes[0].axvline(TREAT_TIME - 0.5, ls="--", c="k"); axes[0].axhline(0, c="k", lw=0.8)
axes[0].set(title="Gaps: treated (red) vs placebo donors", xlabel="period")
ratios = placebos["ratio"].sort_values()
axes[1].barh(range(len(ratios)), ratios, color=["C3" if u == TREATED else "grey" for u in ratios.index])
axes[1].set(title=f"post/pre RMSPE ratio — permutation p = {p_val:.3f}", yticks=[])
plt.show()








Figure 2.3: Placebo-in-space inference: gap paths for the treated market and placebo donors (left) and the ranked post/pre RMSPE ratios (right).





With 30 donors the smallest attainable p-value is 1/31 ≈ 0.032: placebo inference needs a reasonably large donor pool.

2.4 Robustness: leave one donor out
If the result hinges on a single donor (which might have had its own shock), it’s fragile. Drop each donor with positive weight and refit.

    r = synth.synthetic_control(wide.drop(columns=donor), TREATED, TREAT_TIME)
    loo.append({"dropped": donor, "weight_in_full_fit": sc.weights[donor], "ATT": r.att, "pre_rmspe": r.pre_rmspe})

TipWorkflow




plot pre-trends; (2) fit both; (3) compare backtest error; (4) if they agree, report both — agreement is reassuring; if they disagree, the backtest tells you which counterfactual to trust; (5) placebo inference + leave-one-out.









NoteHybrids that bridge the two



Synthetic DiD (Arkhangelsky et al. 2021) adds unit + time weights to DiD; Augmented SC (Ben-Michael et al. 2021) bias-corrects SC with an outcome model when pre-fit is imperfect. Libraries: pysyncon (SC, augmented SC, placebo tests), SparseSC, synthdid ports; Google’s CausalImpact / tfcausalimpact is a Bayesian structural-time-series cousin.

Arkhangelsky, Dmitry, Susan Athey, David A. Hirshberg, Guido W. Imbens, and Stefan Wager. 2021. “Synthetic Difference-in-Differences.” American Economic Review.






WarningPractical gotchas



exclude donors that could receive spillovers (neighbouring markets) or had their own interventions; match on outcome levels and key predictors when the pre-period is short; standardize if outcomes have very different scales across donors.

title: 2  Synthetic Control, and Choosing Between SC and DiD
text:
2.6 Check your understanding






TipWhy isn’t in-sample pre-period fit enough to choose between SC and DiD?





The more flexible method always fits the pre-period better, because its weights are chosen to do exactly that. The backtest holds out the last pre-treatment periods and scores the forecast where the true effect is zero.









TipWhy can’t the placebo p-value go below about 0.03 with 30 donors?





The treated unit is ranked among 31 units (itself plus 30 placebos), so its smallest possible p-value is 1/31 ≈ 0.032.









ImportantTry it



Set TRUE_EFFECT = 0.0 in the data cell and re-render. Does the placebo p-value stay small, and what happens to the backtest comparison?

title: 3  Event Studies
text:
Estimation window (here days −250 to −30): fit \(r_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta_i r_{mt} + \varepsilon_{it}\). The gap before the event keeps leakage/run-up out of the benchmark.
Event window (−5 to +10): abnormal return \(AR_{it} = r_{it} - (\hat\alpha_i + \hat\beta_i r_{mt})\).
Aggregate: average AR by event day (AAR), cumulative AR (CAR1), and cross-sectional tests.

1 CAR: cumulative abnormal return, the sum of a firm’s abnormal returns over a window. CAAR is its average across firms.





NoteSimulated truth



+2% on day 0 and +0.2%/day drift for 5 days, so true CAR[0,+5] = 3.0%.












TipPractical notes: financial event studies




Benchmarks: market model is the workhorse; Fama–French 3/5-factor or industry benchmarks matter for long windows or small caps.
Event-date clustering: if many firms share the same event date (e.g. a regulation), their ARs are cross-correlated and the cross-sectional t-test overstates precision — use portfolio/calendar-time approaches.
Event-induced variance: volatility often spikes on event days; the cross-sectional test used here is robust to that, as is the Boehmer–Musumeci–Poulsen (BMP) standardized test.
Confounding events: screen out firms with other news (earnings + M&A on the same day) in the window.
Long horizons: CARs compound benchmark misspecification; prefer buy-and-hold abnormal returns with matched benchmarks or calendar-time portfolios.

title: 3  Event Studies
section: 3.2 Part B · Staggered rollout of a feature across markets
text:
3.2 Part B · Staggered rollout of a feature across markets
Units adopt in three cohorts (periods 6, 11, 16) plus a never-treated group. The effect differs by cohort (earlier adopters benefit more) and grows by 0.3 per period after adoption.
Why TWFE breaks: with staggered timing, TWFE implicitly uses already-treated units as controls for later adopters. When effects grow over time, those “controls” are still changing because of treatment, contaminating the comparison (Goodman-Bacon 2021; Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille 2020; Sun and Abraham 2021).

Goodman-Bacon, Andrew. 2021. “Difference-in-Differences with Variation in Treatment Timing.” Journal of Econometrics.

Chaisemartin, Clément de, and Xavier D’Haultfœuille. 2020. “Two-Way Fixed Effects Estimators with Heterogeneous Treatment Effects.” American Economic Review.

Sun, Liyang, and Sarah Abraham. 2021. “Estimating Dynamic Treatment Effects in Event Studies with Heterogeneous Treatment Effects.” Journal of Econometrics.

Callaway, Brantly, and Pedro H. C. Sant’Anna. 2021. “Difference-in-Differences with Multiple Time Periods.” Journal of Econometrics.
The fix used here is Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021): estimate each cohort-by-period effect \(ATT(g,t)\) with a clean 2×2 comparison (cohort \(g\) vs never-treated, relative to period \(g-1\)), then aggregate by event time.

The dynamic TWFE event study does better in the middle of the window (a large never-treated group helps), but look at the binned endpoints (−5 and +7): they pool many heterogeneous periods and come out biased, and the spurious −5 lead could be misread as a pre-trend. TipPractical notes: rollout event studies

Rollout order is rarely random: if markets with the best expected gains go first, cohorts differ systematically. Check pre-trends by cohort.
Event-time estimates far from zero are identified from fewer cohorts — show cohort composition or trim the window.
Libraries: csdid (Python port of R did), differences, pyfixest (did2s, saturated event studies), linearmodels.

title: 4  Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)
text:
4.1 Local linear estimate
Setting: treatment is assigned by a strict rule on a continuous running variable: customers with a risk score ≥ 0 get a premium offer, students above a test cutoff get a scholarship, stores above a revenue threshold get a new process.
Units just above and just below the cutoff are nearly identical, so the jump in the outcome at the cutoff is the causal effect for units at the threshold (Equation 4.1):
\[\tau_{RD} = \lim_{x \downarrow c} E[Y \mid X=x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c} E[Y \mid X=x] \tag{4.1}\]
Fit separate linear regressions on each side within bandwidth \(h\), weighting observations closer to the cutoff more (triangular kernel1). The coefficient on the treatment dummy is the jump. Local linear (not local constant) is standard because it has much smaller bias at a boundary.

title: 4  Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)
text:
4.4 Practical notes

Don’t use global high-order polynomials (e.g. a 5th-order fit over the whole range). They give noisy, misleading estimates at the boundary (Gelman and Imbens 2019). Use local linear/quadratic.
Fuzzy RD: if crossing the cutoff only raises the probability of treatment, the jump in the outcome divided by the jump in treatment take-up is a local IV/LATE estimate (rdrobust handles this with fuzzy=).
External validity: the estimate is local to units near the cutoff. Extrapolating to units far away requires extra assumptions.
Discrete running variables (e.g. integer scores) need care — few mass points near the cutoff; see rdrobust/rdlocrand guidance.
Libraries: rdrobust (optimal bandwidths, robust bias-corrected inference), rddensity (Cattaneo–Jansson–Ma density test), rdlocrand (local randomization inference).

title: 5  Propensity-Score Methods
text:
5.1 Estimate the propensity score and check overlap
Setting: observational data — nobody randomized treatment. Example: customers who chose to enroll in a loyalty program; we want the program’s effect on spend. Enrollees differ systematically (more engaged, higher income), so a naive comparison mixes the program effect with selection.
Propensity score: \(e(x) = P(T=1 \mid X=x)\). Rosenbaum and Rubin (1983): if treatment is as-good-as-random given \(X\), it is also as-good-as-random given the scalar \(e(X)\). So we can balance many confounders through one number.
Overlap is the first thing to look at. Regions where one group has (almost) no counterparts are where every estimator extrapolates — IPW weights explode there. Common remedies: trim to a region of common support [e.g. 0.05 < e < 0.95; Crump et al. (2009)], or switch the estimand (ATT, or overlap weights).

title: 5  Propensity-Score Methods
text:
5.3 Estimate the effect several ways

Regression adjustment: model \(E[Y|X,T]\) and average predicted differences. Relies entirely on the outcome model.
IPW: reweight so the treated and control groups each look like the target population. Relies entirely on the propensity model; variance blows up with extreme weights.
Matching (ATT): pair each treated unit with the control closest in (logit) propensity, within a caliper.
AIPW: combines both models; consistent if either is right, and efficient if both are. With cross-fitting it pairs naturally with flexible ML learners (the double/debiased ML recipe).

Bootstrap SEs for IPW and matching; AIPW gets an analytic influence-function SE.


Code
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier, GradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

def regression_adjustment(Xd, yd, td):
    m1 = LinearRegression().fit(Xd[td == 1], yd[td == 1])
    m0 = LinearRegression().fit(Xd[td == 0], yd[td == 0])
    return float(np.mean(m1.predict(Xd) - m0.predict(Xd)))

def bootstrap_se(fn, n_boot=200, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    draws = []
    for _ in range(n_boot):
        i = rng.integers(0, len(df), len(df))
        Xb, yb, tb = X.iloc[i].reset_index(drop=True), y.iloc[i].reset_index(drop=True), t.iloc[i].reset_index(drop=True)
        draws.append(fn(Xb, yb, tb))
    return float(np.std(draws, ddof=1))

ipw_att = lambda Xd, yd, td: ps_lib.ipw(yd, td, ps_lib.fit_propensity(Xd, td), "ATT").estimate
match = lambda Xd, yd, td: ps_lib.match_att(yd, td, ps_lib.fit_propensity(Xd, td), caliper=0.05)[0].estimate

Deliberately break one model at a time. IPW depends only on the propensity model, regression adjustment only on the outcome model — AIPW survives as long as one of them is right.

title: 5  Propensity-Score Methods
text:
5.5 Practical notes

Design before analysis: write down the causal graph; include pre-treatment confounders, exclude mediators and colliders (and instruments, which inflate variance and can amplify bias).
Overlap first, then balance, then estimate. Report how many units were trimmed or unmatched — it changes the population the estimate describes.
Sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding: E-values (VanderWeele & Ding), Rosenbaum bounds, or omitted-variable-bias bounds (Cinelli & Hazlett’s sensemakr). “How strong would a hidden confounder need to be to explain this away?”
Prefer doubly robust + cross-fitting when using ML models for nuisance functions.
Libraries: DoWhy (graph-first workflow + refutation tests), EconML (DML, causal forests, heterogeneous effects), causalml, zEpid.

TipWhy judge a propensity model by balance rather than by AUC?





The model’s job is to balance covariates between the groups, not to predict treatment. A highly predictive model can mean poor overlap. Check that |SMD| falls below about 0.1 after weighting.









TipWhat does double robustness guarantee, and what doesn’t it?





AIPW is consistent if either the outcome model or the propensity model is correct. It fails when both are wrong, and it cannot fix a confounder you never measured.

title: 6  Geo Experiments and Switchback Testing
text:
6.1 Part A · Interference: a user-level A/B test in a supply-constrained marketplace
User-level A/B tests assume SUTVA1: one user’s treatment doesn’t affect another’s outcome. That breaks in:
Two standard fixes randomize at a coarser level so spillovers stay inside a unit of randomization:
Part A shows why user-level tests mislead under interference. Part B designs and analyses a matched-pair geo experiment. Part C runs a switchback with carryover.
Users request orders; there are only 3,000 couriers-worth of capacity per day. A promo lifts treated users’ request rate from 20% to 26%. When demand exceeds supply, requests are filled at random — so treated users’ extra orders displace control users’ orders.
Code
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N_USERS, CAPACITY, P_CTRL, P_TREAT, DAYS = 20_000, 3_000, 0.20, 0.26, 30

def simulate_day(treat_mask):
    wants = rng.random(N_USERS) < np.where(treat_mask, P_TREAT, P_CTRL)
    requesters = np.flatnonzero(wants)
    filled = np.zeros(N_USERS, bool)
    filled[rng.choice(requesters, size=min(CAPACITY, len(requesters)), replace=False)] = True
    return filled

ab_lift, global_t, global_c = [], [], []
for _ in range(DAYS):
    half = rng.random(N_USERS) < 0.5
    f = simulate_day(half)
    ab_lift.append(f[half].mean() / f[~half].mean() - 1)
    global_t.append(simulate_day(np.ones(N_USERS, bool)).sum())
    global_c.append(simulate_day(np.zeros(N_USERS, bool)).sum())

print(f"User-level A/B estimate of order lift:      {np.mean(ab_lift):+.1%}")
print(f"True market-level effect (all-on vs all-off): {np.mean(global_t) / np.mean(global_c) - 1:+.1%}")


User-level A/B estimate of order lift:      +31.4%
True market-level effect (all-on vs all-off): +0.0%
The A/B test reports a ~30% lift that doesn’t exist at market level: the platform was supply-bound, so the promo only reshuffled who got served. Randomizing whole markets (Part B) or whole time periods (Part C) puts both “worlds” under the same capacity constraint and measures the real, global effect.

6.2 Part B · Matched-pair geo experiment
Design. 40 geos with 90 days of pre-period history. Pair geos with similar pre-period volume, randomize one of each pair to treatment. Pairing on a strong predictor dramatically improves precision when you only have tens of units.
Analysis. Time-Based Regression (TBR; Kerman et al. (2017)): regress aggregate treatment-group sales on aggregate control-group sales during the pre-period, forecast the post-period counterfactual, and sum the difference. Complemented by randomization inference over the actual pair design.

6.2.1 Power check before launch: A/A backtests on history
Run the full analysis many times on pre-period data only, with fresh random pair assignments and a fake test window where the true effect is zero. The spread of these placebo estimates is the noise floor; the minimum detectable effect (80% power, α = 0.10 two-sided) is roughly 2.5 × that SD.

    aa.append(summ["relative_lift"])

TipGeo-experiment practicalities




Spillover across borders: commuters and media markets leak. Use DMA-level geos, add buffer zones, or exclude border geos.

6.3 Part C · Switchback test with carryover
Randomize treatment by time block in one market (e.g. a new dispatch algorithm on/off in 4-hour blocks for 8 weeks). Everyone in the market is in the same regime at the same time, so interference between users is contained.
The catch is carryover: supply repositions slowly, so the system takes a few hours to reach the new regime after each switch. Measured right after a switch, outcomes reflect partly the previous regime, biasing the estimate toward zero.






NoteSimulated truth



the steady-state (always-on vs always-off) effect is +8 on an hourly metric; exposure adjusts with persistence 0.6 per hour.




Code
TRUE_SB_EFFECT, HOURS = 8.0, 24 * 56

def run_switchback(block_len, seed):
    a = experiments.switchback_assignment(HOURS, block_len, seed=seed)
    d = simulate.switchback_marketplace(a.assignment.to_numpy(), effect=TRUE_SB_EFFECT, persistence=0.6, seed=seed)
    return pd.concat([d, a[["block", "since_switch"]]], axis=1)

sb = run_switchback(block_len=4, seed=1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.5))
w = sb[sb.t < 24 * 3]
ax.step(w.t, w.treated * TRUE_SB_EFFECT, where="post", c="grey", label="assignment (scaled)")
ax.plot(w.t, w.exposure * TRUE_SB_EFFECT, c="C3", label="effective treatment (with carryover)")
ax.set(title="Carryover: the system lags behind the assignment", xlabel="hour"); ax.legend(); plt.show()

TipSwitchback practicalities




Estimate carryover first (e.g. from an earlier test or system dynamics) and set burn-in ≥ the time to reach a new steady state.
